extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent litigators, patent practitioners, in-house counsel defending utility patent suits
extracted.subtask_description: Practical underutilized defenses and argumentative approaches a defendant can raise in U.S. utility patent litigation (focus on claim construction, indefiniteness, damages mitigation, and public-domain issues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Steps without Acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Method claim elements that recite only a function/’step’ without reciting the acts by which that function is performed can trigger §112(f) treatment (means/step-plus-function) and may be invalid if the specification fails to disclose acts sufficient to perform the function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory text: 35 U.S.C. §112(f) allows an element 'expressed as a means or step for performing a specified function without the recital of structure, material, or acts in support thereof' to be construed to cover corresponding structure/material/acts in the specification and equivalents. Judge Rader: 'underlying function' corresponds to what the element accomplishes; 'acts' correspond to how the function is accomplished. If a claim element recites only an underlying function without acts, §112, ¶6 may apply even absent express step-plus-function language. Practical approach: for each method step, ask whether it recites acts that perform the function or only the function/result; if only the latter, analyze the specification to see whether it discloses and links acts sufficient to perform the function. Examples/case citations: Seal-Flex (Rader concurrence), O.I. Corp. v. Tekmar, Dionex Softron (non-precedential) and related §101 decisions (Internet Patents Corp.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefiniteness stemming from unclear application of §112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: When it is unclear whether claim language invokes §112(f), the scope of the claim is uncertain and that ambiguity can render the claim indefinite under §112(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical approach: if arguing that a limitation triggers §112(f), also argue alternatively that uncertainty as to whether §112(f) applies renders the limitation indefinite under §112(b). The USPTO/Examiner guidance (MPEP §2181 I) instructs examiners that if it's unclear whether a limitation falls within 112(f), a rejection under 112(b) may be appropriate. Emphasize that invoking or contesting §112(f) affects how broadly a limitation is interpreted and thus can be fertile ground for indefiniteness arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to Mitigate Damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent owners, like plaintiffs in other torts, have a duty to mitigate damages; failure to take reasonable steps to avoid or minimize damages can reduce or preclude recovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal principle: patent infringement is a tort and is presumptively governed by common law tort damages principles (e.g., Staub v. Proctor Hospital). The victim/plaintiff has a duty to use reasonable means to avoid or minimize damages; failure to do so can limit recovery. Illustrative actions by patent owners that may constitute failure to mitigate include failure to mark patented products, 'lying in wait' while damages accrue, failing to take a clear or consistent position on claim scope, keeping a licensed supplier secret, or failing to offer a FRAND license when obligated. Case references: Faragher (background on mitigation principles), Bank of Stockton (example under state law). Practical approach: investigate patent owner conduct and plead/argue failure to mitigate as a defense to damages, presenting evidence of reasonable steps that could have reduced harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expiring Patents Add to the Public Domain
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosures in expired (non-asserted) patents are in the public domain; accused features described in such expired patents may not be proprietary and can reduce or eliminate liability or damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal principle and cases: expired patents dedicate their disclosed inventions to the public (Bonito Boats; Scott Paper; Singer Mfg.); courts recognize that the public may use the invention and obvious or indistinct modifications (Gilead). Practical effects: identify expired patents that describe part or all of the claimed subject matter and assert that those disclosures are free for public use; even if not a complete defense, such public-domain disclosures may reduce damages by excluding value attributable to material in the public domain. Use apportionment principles (e.g., AstraZeneca v. Apotex on accounting for conventional vs. unconventional elements) to argue exclusion of public-domain-contributed value from damages.
